chapter_theme: On the wedding night the groom goes up to the mansion with the maid, is drawn to her shy beauty, and speaks his wonder and servitude to her, before he goes down into the play grove where young women sing warnings to the plants about her beauty, and then climbs back up.

cast.role: the young lord who saw the picture and fell in love and is now the groom; the epithets காளை, விடலை and வேலான் are taken to name him
the bride, the Vidyadhara king's daughter, unnamed in these verses
the bees he tells to keep away from her hair
the young women who sing warnings to the plants, named only at 1129
the sweet mango tree addressed in the song
the kurukkatti creeper addressed in the song
the fragrant kurava tree addressed in the song
the attendants who bow at his feet

1108.reading: At the drum's proclamation he has jewels and gold showered on petitioners until their wishes are filled, then climbs the tall guarded mansion with the maid, and the poet calls him the form of the joy the world at its end attains.
1108.nuance: The giving comes first and the climb to the bride's bed second, so the wedding night opens with the king's bounty before it turns private; the last line's praise of the youth is compressed.
1108.event: He has gold and jewels rained on petitioners at a drum's proclamation, then climbs the tall mansion with the maid.

1109.reading: The garlanded woman and the youth take their couch at the top of the mansion, where the smoke of burning fragrant wood gathers like dark cloud, and they look like a divine pair mounting a jewelled peak.
1109.nuance: Reading காக துண்டம் as a burning aromatic wood is my inference from the verse's cloud and fragrance images.
1109.event: The couple go up to their couch on the mansion's roof.

1110.reading: The shy girl lies down on the flower bed, he gazes till his eyes are glad, draws her as she shrinks and presses her to his broad chest, and says he longs to hear her sweet laughing lisp.
1110.nuance: The spoken words are given only as 'என்கொலோ என்று', so what he asks is only half stated.
1110.event: The youth draws the shrinking girl to his chest and asks to hear her voice.

1111.reading: The cage of her shame breaks open as his mountain-like arms close on her, and she, like a nectar-river, sinks in the sea of his ardour.
1111.nuance: Shame is made a cage (சிறை) from which she is released, and the one who sinks is the river, not the sea; the figure of river and sea is compressed and several details are read loosely.
1111.event: The maiden's shame gives way and she is taken into the youth's embrace.

1112.reading: Like a bud that by its season opens, ripens and bears fruit, they come to the sweet food of desire and cannot take enough of it, and are two in body but one in heart.
1112.nuance: The ripening bud-flower-fruit image makes the union a growth over time and not an event of one night; the last line states the oneness of heart as the result.
1112.event: The couple consummate their love and are joined in heart.

1113.reading: His garland and her pearl strings tangle on his chest, and union, delight and playful sulking blend until they fall into a daze like drinkers of honey-wine.
1113.nuance: புலவி is named in one list with union and delight, with no quarrel and no cause given, so the sulk here is part of the pleasure and not a breach.
1113.event: The couple lose themselves in union and play.

1114.reading: He sets her ornaments right, smooths her coiled hair, crowns her with a flower, embraces her as her smile buds, seats her on his lap and speaks the words that follow so she may hear.
1114.event: The youth adorns the bride, seats her on his lap and begins to speak to her.

1115.reading: He says her body smells of the red lily and her red mouth of the same and of the water lily, and that the god who first made her made his life her servant.
1115.nuance: The maker (தேவன்) as the cause of his bondage is a lover's way of speaking, a small echo of fate in a verse of praise; no claim about karma is made.

1116.reading: He says the doe-eyed doll lit the fire of melting love that burns his bones, and that she is the sweet nectar the old sea bore, taken as a slim form.
1116.nuance: Fire and nectar are said of the same woman, the paradox that verse 1118 develops.

1117.reading: He says her long eyes are the arrows with which the lord of the hot season won, that Kama must have done austerity for his victory, and that he himself has done austerity for this long to touch her fragrant body.
1117.nuance: நோற்றான் and நோற்றேன் are the words of vows and penance; here a lover turns them to the wish to touch his bride, which a Jain reader would hear against the epic's own austerities. Verse 986 already gave Prajapati's words that the winner of such a bride must have great earlier austerity.

claims.claim: union with the beloved is the reward of austerity done before

1118.reading: He says the dark-eyed girl has become the nectar he eats as a guest, his very life and his rare medicine, while he, a sinner, has become servant to a doll.
1118.nuance: பாவியேன் is the lover's self-reproach in play and not a charge of wrongdoing; the same woman is feast, life and medicine at once.

1119.reading: He says it would be enough to look at her coral-red small feet and worship them, but at the sight of her red mouth and curl-crowded brow he loses himself and cannot say why it is his sin.
1119.nuance: வழிபடுவது, the word of worship, is used for her feet; the last line is hard and its sense is uncertain.

1120.reading: He tells the bees that sat in her braided hair and troubled her slim waist not to come to her tender body's fragrance as before.
1120.nuance: The middle lines are compressed, and who is hurt by whom is read from the context of a bridegroom guarding his bride.

1121.reading: He says the sly-eyed girl has hidden herself, and when he tries to hold her in his heart he cannot see her form, and he does not know what his unsatisfied longing has come upon.
1121.nuance: Even with her in his arms he looks for her in his heart; the closing lines are corrupt or compressed.

1122.reading: He says that even when she sits lovingly on his lap she looks like a stranger each time he blinks, so he will gaze unblinking at her flower-like face, and he knows not how he will live while his beloved is shy.
1122.nuance: Her shame still stands after the embrace of 1111, and he reads it as a distance he fears.

1123.reading: He, with shoulders like a rock, praises her beauty and is like a monsoon storm that makes the young jasmine open, and she like the jasmine vine that is the pride of her line.
1123.nuance: The two similes cast the couple as storm and flower, with the storm as the active one.

1124.reading: Her flower-garlanded, carp-like eyes take him captive, and the spear-bearing youth, his mind lost, no longer behaves with his attendants as before and goes into the pleasure grove.
1124.event: The youth, lost in her eyes, enters the play grove.

1125.reading: Under the red asoka whose tender leaves hang with bees, he climbs onto a jewelled round seat, plays with his beloved and hears the music sung by the women.
1125.nuance: பிண்டி, the asoka, is the tree under which the Jina is said to have won omniscience in Jain tradition, so the play takes place in the Jina's own shade; the last line's relation of the women to him is unclear.
1125.event: In the grove he plays with the bride and listens to the singing women.

1126.reading: The singers tell the sweet mango not to put out sprouts that borrow the colour of the mountain king's daughter, for in the spring wind it will bear scars and rows of fruit and be plucked.
1126.nuance: வடு means both young fruit and scar, and the warning may play on both; the speakers are named only in 1129.
1126.event: The young women sing to the mango tree, warning it not to rival the bride's colour.

1127.reading: The singers tell the kurukkatti creeper, long may it live, not to take the grace of the vine-waisted chief queen of the wheel-ruler whom kings bow to, for if it does many will pluck it and it will not bloom in the guarded garden.
1127.nuance: The bride is called the great queen of the lord who rules the wheel, so the song already gives her the title Prajapati's words at 986 foretold.
1127.event: The singers warn the kurukkatti creeper not to match the queen's grace.

1128.reading: The singers tell the fragrant kurava tree not to grow as lovely as the loving daughter of the king whom the world bows to, for if it does the young men will pluck it in crowds.
1128.event: The singers warn the kurava tree that being as fragrant as the bride will bring it plucking.

1129.reading: Hearing the young women sing, a smile like moonlight flashes for a moment on the king's daughter's face, and the youth's eyes drink it in.
1129.nuance: The smile is not said to answer the song, only to follow it.
1129.event: The bride smiles at the song and the youth's eyes take it in.

1130.reading: As attendants bow at his feet and the bright-earringed bride's radiance holds his mind, the lion-like youth climbs the cloud-brushing pillared mansion.
1130.event: The youth goes back up to the tall mansion.

links.note: 1111 shows her shame breaking like a cage; 1122 shows her still shy and stranger-like in his lap.
links.teaches: The bride's shame is not undone in one embrace, and the groom still feels the distance it leaves after the cage is said to be broken.

links.note: 1112 makes two bodies one heart by ripening; Kural 1122 says the bond is as body is to life.
links.teaches: The epic gives the oneness of lovers a history of slow ripening, while the couplet states only the result as a bond of body and life.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a measure of how total the oneness is, as between body and life, which its bud-and-fruit figure does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gets a story in which the bond grows from bud to fruit instead of being given.

links.note: 1111 has the groom's ardour carry her shame off; Kural 1134 has the flood of love carry off the raft of shame and manliness.
links.teaches: The same flood that costs the secret lover his standing in the Kural is blessed here, because the epic's shame falls away inside a wedding.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's naming of shame as something love sweeps away, and so as a loss, which its cage image hides.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where losing shame costs nothing, showing the loss it names depends on love outside marriage.

links.note: 1113 mixes union, delight and sulking in one daze; Kural 1109 lists sulking, making up and union as love's fruits in order.
links.teaches: The epic blends what the couplet puts in a sequence, so the sulk is a flavour inside union and not a stage before it.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's claim that the sulk is itself a reward of love, which explains why it sits in a list of pleasures.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where the three do not follow each other but occur together, without any making up needed.

links.note: 1113 lets the pair dissolve in a daze of union; Tirumanthiram 1960 teaches union in which the bindu is kept and infatuation dies.
links.teaches: The epic gives the surrender that Tirumular's discipline of union is set against, and the Saiva verse asks what the daze costs.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a question it never asks, whether the daze of union is a loss, and a measure by which a yogi would judge it.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gets the householder's full surrender as the ordinary case its restraint is defined against.

links.note: 986 says whoever wins the bride must have great earlier austerity; 1117 has the groom claim he did austerity to touch her.
links.teaches: The groom's claim fulfils the father's prediction and turns the language of penance from release to desire.

links.note: 1022 has the youth fear her glance as an arrow that will kill him; 1117 takes her eyes as the arrows and his austerity as their reward.
links.teaches: The same arrow that the fear of the picture-scene dreads is accepted as the prize of the wedding night.

links.note: 1118 makes the girl both his life and his rare medicine and him her servant; Kural 1102 says she is the cure for the sickness she brings.
links.teaches: The cure is a bondage in the epic, since the groom who is healed is enslaved by what heals him.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the argument behind its list of titles, that a cure ordinarily differs from its cause but here is the same person.
gains.b: The couplet gets a sequel in which the cure becomes servitude, which its single line leaves open.

links.note: 1037 compares the lotus and the worshippers of the Jina's feet to the maiden's red feet; 1119 has the groom call worship of those feet enough.
links.teaches: The poet moves the worship of feet from the Jina to the bride through the groom's mouth and so shows love borrowing a devotional form.

links.note: 1122 has him gaze unblinking so as not to lose her; Kural 1129 has her not blink lest he be hidden.
links.teaches: The refusal to blink is common to both lovers, but the epic's reason is that she seems to recede each time he blinks, and the Kural's is that he lives in her eye.

gains.a: The epic verse gets proof that not blinking is a common sign of love, said by the woman in the Kural and by the man here.
gains.b: The couplet gets the groom's reverse case, where the fear is that she herself becomes a stranger at each blink.

links.note: 986 says the winner of the bride will surely rule the wheel; 1127 calls her the great queen of the wheel-ruler.
links.teaches: The singers speak as if the father's prophecy were already true, so the wedding is also the first coronation of her place.

links.note: 1128 warns the kurava tree not to grow as fragrant as the bride, lest it be plucked; Kural 1111 greets the anicham flower and says the beloved is more delicate.
links.teaches: Praising a girl by comparing her to a flower carries a threat in the epic, where equalling her gets the flower plucked, and only flattery in the couplet.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's form of speaking to a flower, so that its warning can be heard as a courtly praise.
gains.b: The couplet gets a darker side to the comparison, since a flower that equals her is in danger.

links.note: 1128 closes the songs' warnings about being plucked; 1129 shows the bride's smile after hearing them.
links.teaches: The songs tease the groom as the one who plucks, and the smile is the only answer given.

links.note: 1108 has him climb the tall mansion with the maid; 1130 has him climb the cloud-high mansion again after the grove.
links.teaches: The two climbs enclose the grove as an interlude, so the chapter starts and ends on the mansion where the wedding night is held.

source_issues: Verses 1110, 1127 and 1128 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four lines.
Verse 1110 had a stray pulli on a line repaired.
Word division is broken in many verses of this chapter, and several readings in 1119 to 1125 are held loosely.
